# Trengtreng walks into a disaster resilience & recovery firm

Walk into any disaster resilience & recovery outfit and watch for ten minutes. You will see a very old act performed with newer props. The act has a name. It is **Trengtreng**.

## Before the Office, the Story

**The Flood and the Volcanic Pillars.** Mapuche tradition tells of a primordial deluge driven by Caicai Vilu, the water-serpent, enemy of the earth-serpent Trentren and of humankind.  As Caicai made the sea rise to drown the world, Trentren raised the hills in answer, each power straining against the other until the mountains out-topped the waters; the peaks of Trengtreng and Kai-Kai became refuges above the flood, while above the serpents stood Pillán, lord of volcano and storm.  Those who reached the heights survived and became the ancestors of the Mapuche.

**Pillán and the Sacred Heights.** Pillán, the Mapuche thunder-and-volcano spirit, is the power whose name crackles in storms and whose fire runs down the cordillera.  The voice of the volcano is his voice, its eruption his weapon; the chroniclers describe the thunder spirits waging war from the heights with fire and storm.  Trengtreng belongs to his storm-world twice over — as one of the peaks raised in the flood-duel, and as a name that rattles like the thunder it imitates — which is why colonial sources sometimes blur the mountain, the thunder-sound, and the god into a single figure.

## The Reveal, Seat by Seat

## Not the First Rebrand

Colonial Spanish missionaries interpreted Mapuche thunder spirits through Christian ideas of divine punishment, while Mapuche communities resisted by preserving Pillan and Trengtreng in oral tradition and ritual. The reduplicated thunder name parallels onomatopoeic storm words across the Andes, and the figure of a deity who raises mountains during a world flood has affinities with widespread South American cosmologies of catastrophe and renewal. The office is only the latest translation.
